title: Identity in the database
subtitle: How the Keycloak user reaches every audit row
summary: A connection pool signs in as one database account, yet every audit row names the real person. ActorAwareDataSource runs SET @app_actor = ?, @request_id = ? on every connection it hands out, and the audit and version triggers read those session variables.

sections.title: ActorAwareDataSource
What it enables
items: Core's Audit Trail filters by actor across all schemas: registrar, service-account-svc-racing, system:licence-expiry.
The request id ties a UI action, its service calls and their audit rows together (X-Request-Id, also sent by TurfBot as turfbot-<conversation>-<question>).
Version triggers increment version_no so optimistic locking works even for changes made outside JPA.

episode.title: Who really changed that row? Propagating identity to MySQL
episode.hook: The database user is always 'turfclub'. The audit trail still says 'registrar'. Here is the trick.
